episodes.213444: A stationary front stationed across central Pennsylvania allowed for a lifting mechanism for showers and storms during the morning and afternoon hours of July 5, 2026. Showers and isolated thunderstorms began to develop across portions of western and central Pennsylvaia during the late morning hours and began to exhibit slow forward motion and instances of training. This continued into the afternoon and evening hours, where heavy rainfall persisted over Tyrone in Blair County for upwards of an hour. This prompted considerable flash flooding in the borough, with multiple homes being flooded and some roadways taking on between two and three feet of water. There were also two children that were rescued from flood waters near the paper mill in Tyrone due to the flooding. Given the unstable airmass, thunderstorms continued to grow upscale throughout the afternoon and evening hours, producing multiple instances of tree damage across Centre, Mifflin and Franklin Counties. As storms shifted eastward, favorable low-level shear allowed for some storms to form into a line with some areas of rotation, one of which prompted the Lambs Gap EF-1 Tornado in Perry County. This line continued to move eastward and produced multiple instances of wind damage and flash flooding in Cumberland, Dauphin, and Lancaster Counties throughout the evening before shifting east of the region.
episodes.213472: Excessive heat and humidity allowed thunderstorms to grow tall enough to produce damaging winds.
episodes.213535: Afternoon thunderstorm activity beneath a ridge of high pressure over New Mexico exhibited relatively short life cycles, but still capable of brief periods of localized heavy rainfall. This combined with the severe to extreme drought conditions over the area allowing for soil and dirt to be readily erodible with one such storm producing an inch or more along Highway 52 south of the Very Large Array (VLA) in southwestern Socorro County. This produced flash flooding over the dirt roadway, shutting down the road for a period of time into the next day.

episodes.213620: The stationary front that caused numerous instances of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding on July 5th continues to linger over central Pennsylvania into July 6, 2026. The environment over central Pennsylvania did possess slightly less instability and shear compared to previous days; however, sufficient instability within a moist environment and a lifting mechanism allowed for some scattered showers and storms to develop during the late afternoon hours. These storms mainly formed across northwestern Pennsylvania, where multiple rounds of locally heavy rainfall caused flash flooding in McKean and Elk Counties before shifting further southward as showers and storms congealed into a line with the bulk of severe activity shifting towards western Pennsylvania. Heavy rainfall still caused multiple instances of flash flooding in Clearfield County as well before shifting further south into Centre and Blair Counties and resulting in multiple instances of flash flooding during the evening hours. The most considerable flooding happened further northeast, in the village of Potter Brook, Tioga County, where multiple homes were evacuated due to water up to the first floor and multiple roadways were impassable.
episodes.213622: A weak shortwave neared the Upstate of SC early in the day with surface troughing already evident into the Midlands of SC by the mid morning. Surface dewpoints were in the mid 70s much of the day, with MLCAPE values up to 2500-3000 J/kg developing by the late morning. This lead to a cluster of severe thunderstorms over Lexington and Richland Counties during the late morning that brought scattered tree damage, including a likely microburst near the Forest Acres neighborhood in Columbia. Efficient rainfall also brought an isolated instance of flash flooding in Lexington County. Recovery ensued the remainder of the day with another round of thunderstorms bringing damaging wind gusts during the evening across the southeastern Midlands into the Pee Dee. The evening thunderstorms also brought a copious amount of lightning with the Newberry County Sheriff reporting that the EOC building was struck by lightning, causing communications to go down.
episodes.213733: Slow moving storms anchored along the terrain in western Allegany County, Maryland producing a quick two to three inches of rain in about an hour. Additionally, a stationary storm produced two to four inches of rain over Montgomery County, Maryland. This resulted in isolated instances of flash flooding.
episodes.213735: A slow moving boundary resulted in showers and thunderstorms that produced a localized two to four inches of rain.
episodes.213769: Slow moving thunderstorms along a frontal boundary produced localized rainfall totals of two to four inches. episodes.213808: A small microburst on July 5 in Eclectic in Elmore County blew trees down around town. The next afternoon, lightning struck a home in Northport in Tuscaloosa County, resulting in an injury.
episodes.213947: Another weather disturbance moved through the combined Panhandles on July 5th. Showers and thunderstorms were able to develop during the evening hours, some moving in from the west. The combination of storms and residual outflow boundaries combined to initiate a more organized line of storms that moved through the Amarillo area. These storms were efficient at producing heavy rainfall, which led to some flooding issues of both poor drainage locations but also vulnerable flooding locations.
episodes.214061: Strong thunderstorms moved through Petroleum and McCone Counties, a few of which became severe.
episodes.214115: Scattered thunderstorms developed across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the late afternoon and evening of the 6th. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.214191: Clusters of thunderstorms developed in the afternoon hours due to an approaching cold front and inland trough. Some of these became severe and produced damaging winds, as well as hail up to quarter size.
episodes.214194: Storms developed along a stationary boundary north of the area during the afternoon of the 5th. These storms developed an outflow boundary which pushed into our area. Storms developing on this outflow boundary produced damaging winds. Even when this boundary outran convection, it still produced severe winds and temporary brown-out conditions due to dust carried by the strong winds.
episodes.214218: Heavy slow moving thunderstorms produced some flash flooding on the Outer Banks during the evening hours.
episodes.214251: A frontal boundary settled into the area early on July 5th. Weak low pressure developed along this front and moved into Northwest Ohio the morning of July 5th. This low pressure then remained nearly stationary through the 5th and into the 6th before weakening and exiting to the southeast later on the 6th into the 7th. The front and low pressure combined with a weak trough aloft to encourage periods of showers and thunderstorms from the 5th through the 6th. A warm and very humid airmass combined with weak steering flow to support slow-moving thunderstorms with torrential rainfall rates. There were a few different waves of thunderstorms with heavy rain. An initial batch of thunderstorms tracked across northern Ohio during the morning and early afternoon of the 5th, bringing flash flooding and severe weather to the Youngstown area. An EF-1 tornado and macroburst caused extensive wind damage across Mahoning County, leading to widespread power outages and a state of emergency declaration. Additional thunderstorms the evening of the 5th brought flash flooding across North Central Ohio. Lake enhanced showers and thunderstorms developed over Lake Erie overnight July 5th into the 6th, with east-northeast winds pushing this activity towards the western lakeshore. The most notable impacts came on Kelleys Island, where 10 to 15 inches of rain fell over a several hour period and led to significant flash flooding during the early morning hours of the 6th. Additional flooding occurred later in the morning and into the afternoon on the mainland from just south of Toledo to the Port Clinton area, with more storms developing during the afternoon and causing flash flooding east of Cleveland in parts of Lake and Geauga Counties.

However over this period of time, damaging winds, large hail, and flash flooding would be noted across much of the state.
episodes.214843: A low pressure system stalled out across the Ohio Valley region sparking rounds of showers and thunderstorms.

episodes.215161: Weak low level steering flow resulting in usual daytime convection driven by both the Gulf and Atlantic sea breezes. Very high instability and layer moisture allowed for numerous showers and thunderstorms, with a few storms becoming locally severe across northeast FL.
episodes.215418: Isolated thunderstorms developed across southeast South Carolina in the early evening hours. One storm in Berkeley County produced strong wind gusts and a few isolated instances of wind damage.
episodes.215423: A large cluster of thunderstorms developed across Berkeley County and produced intense rainfall. Several CoCoRaHS observers in Moncks Corner reported rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches, including a peak amount of 4.86 inches at SC-BK-121 (Moncks Corner 1.0 NNW). The heavy rainfall caused flash flooding in Moncks Corner.
episodes.215486: A shortwave moved through Wyoming and brought severe thunderstorms to Natrona County. In Casper, up to quarter sized hail fell. A wind gust of 59 mph was recorded in Bar Nunn.
episodes.215488: Clusters of thunderstorms developed out ahead of a slow moving cold front located along the border of North Carolina and Virginia during the late morning hours of July sixth. Thunderstorms initially developed near the Alligator river and Albemarle sound and slowly tracked south towards the Croatan and Roanoke sounds. With ample instability and shear a few of these storms became severe in nature bringing damaging wind gusts to portions of the northern sounds during the afternoon.
episodes.215624: A weak midlevel weather system paired with bountiful moisture helped fire numerous scattered showers and thunderstorms. A couple of storms produced heavy rainfall and strong to severe winds in isolated locations.
episodes.216049: Scattered to numerous showers and storms developed in the afternoon through late evening hours across central North Carolina. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed, as well as a few isolated reports of flash flooding.
episodes.216066: Thunderstorms developed over the Pine Ridge of northern Sheridan County during the afternoon hours of July 6th. This activity initiated in the vicinity of a surface trough. As it moved east into better low level moisture, storms became severe over northeastern Sheridan County. Other severe storms tracked through Garden County producing a wind gust to 60 MPH. Elsewhere, 60 MPH winds were reported in Keya Paha County with wind damage to trees reported south of Clinton in Sheridan County.
episodes.216104: An upper-level disturbance brought showers and thunderstorms to Southwest and Central MT. Although the environment for severe thunderstorms was marginal, isolated severe wind gusts and hail developed in mainly terrain driven areas.
episodes.216131: A lightning strike near Dade City in Pasco County critically injured one person and led to another person needing medical transport and treatment.
episodes.216192: Over the course of several days between July 6th and July 9th, an unsettled pattern persisted across the Ohio and Tennessee Valley as a cutoff low meandered across the region. A humid, unstable environment was present throughout this time period with dew point temperatures in the mid 70s and precipitable water values near or exceeding 2 inches. On top of this, relatively weak steering flow in the mid-levels of the atmosphere lead to slow movement of showers and thunderstorms which developed, resulting in localized heavy rainfall amounts and flash flooding. Scattered flash flooding occurred across central Kentucky over the four day period, with severe weather impacts mainly being limited to isolated downbursts from hydrometeor loading in otherwise disorganized cells. However, by the 9th, the ingestion of the cutoff low into broader troughing did provide for slightly stronger wind shear and better storm organization. With a seasonably humid and unstable environment remaining in place, this stronger wind shear did promote a bit more coverage of strong to severe storms, with a couple wind damage reports and a spin-up tornado being observed during the evening and early nighttime hours on July 9th.
episodes.216336: A surface trough and associated frontal boundary led to the development of thunderstorms across western and north central North Dakota during the afternoon and evening. The largest hail report was golf ball sized hail near Loraine in Renville County. Strong thunderstorm wind gusts up to 60 mph were reported in Dunn County at Little Missouri State Park, with small tree branches down.
episodes.216372: A nearly stationary frontal boundary was stretched across the northern tier of PA in a very moist atmosphere with light winds aloft, setting the stage for some slow-moving, heavy showers and embedded thunderstorms during the night of Sunday, the 5th. An area of low pressure moved along this frontal boundary, which helped organize the rain and embedded storms into a broad area of heavy rainfall across portions of Northeast Pennsylvania with localized amounts of 2-5 inches, resulting in areas of flash flooding.
episodes.216509: Active weather stretched through the Independence Day weekend amid oppressive heat and tropical moisture, leading to daily showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. High pressure initially over the region began to condense on July 3rd, which allowed for isolated storms to form along the higher terrain. Coverage then grew in earnest on the 4th of July and then again on the 5th as convective temperatures were breached in the afternoon and scattered storms formed across the state. Storms materialized just before noon across the Kanawha Valley each day and slowly traveled eastward, causing tree and power line damage in its path. The slow movement of these storms also imposed localized flash flooding by July 5th, causing flooded roadways across parts of Boone and Logan Counties. Storms were tied to daytime heating and quickly lost composure after sunset each night as a result, bringing the severe and flooding risks to an end.
episodes.216513: The Independence Day holiday weekend featured an ongoing heat wave, coupled with daily chance of showers and thunderstorms. Precipitation chances increased with each passing day as departing high pressure lost influence over the area. Strong daytime heating and tropical moisture ushering into the region helped to support quick developing storms during the afternoons, which faded with the loss of daytime heating each evening. In southeast Ohio, main implications from these storms were the strong winds that produced tree and power line damage on both July 4th and 5th.
episodes.216515: Modest daytime heating and instability combined with an incoming upper level disturbance led to the development of scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms during the afternoon hours on the 6th. A very moisture-rich atmosphere was in place setting the stage for locally heavy rainfall. Convection was nearly stationary over western Steuben County leading to localized flash flooding with rainfall totals around 3 inches and several reports of 2 inch per hour rainfall totals.
episodes.216533: Active weather was observed on a daily basis in West Virginia from July 6th to the 9th amid hot temperatures and ample moisture. Showers and strong thunderstorms fired up quickly each afternoon, filled with heavy downpours and damaging wind gusts. Downed trees and power lines were the main impacts with severe weather during this stretch of time, along with street flooding and creeks rising out of their banks. The active weather pattern stretched further into the month due to an encroaching frontal boundary that stalled over the region. Daily showers and storms then continued over West Virginia heading into the middle of the month.
episodes.216609: A weakness in the ridge aloft and the presence of a remnant outflow boundary (a result of decaying convection across Oklahoma) led to scattered thunderstorms during the afternoons of July 5th and 6th. Damaging wind gusts were the most common severe weather occurrence, especially at Olney Municipal Airport in Young County where millions of dollars of damage occurred, though a few reports of large hail were also received.
episodes.216816: Thunderstorms produced strong to severe wind gusts along the Brevard County coast.
episodes.216818: Thunderstorms produced a severe wind gust and roadway flooding in northern Brevard County.
episodes.216829: The continued presence of a weak upper level disturbance that lingered across East Texas and North Louisiana on July 6th again focused adequate large scale ascent within a hot, moist, and unstable air mass for scattered severe thunderstorms to develop across portions of East Texas and North Louisiana during the mid and late afternoon hours. These storms produced damaging winds which downed trees and power lines, as well as isolated instances of large hail, before diminishing during the evening.
episodes.216834: The continued presence of a weak upper level disturbance that lingered across East Texas and North Louisiana on July 6th again focused adequate large scale ascent within a hot, moist, and unstable air mass for scattered severe thunderstorms to develop across portions of East Texas, extreme Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana during the mid and late afternoon hours. One isolated severe thunderstorm produced large hail just south of Fouke in Southern Miller County, with the more concentrated areas of severe thunderstorms producing damaging winds and large hail more common to the west over adjacent East Texas, and to the southeast across North Louisiana before diminishing during the evening.
episodes.216835: The continued presence of a weak upper level disturbance that lingered across East Texas and North Louisiana on July 6th again focused adequate large scale ascent within a hot, moist, and unstable air mass for scattered severe thunderstorms to develop across portions of East Texas and North Louisiana during the mid and late afternoon hours. These storms produced damaging winds which downed trees and power lines, as well as isolated instances of large hail, before diminishing during the evening.
episodes.216866: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the Big Country and Concho Valley. Some of the storms were severe and mainly produced wind damage.
episodes.216881: On July 6th, the Weather Prediction Center (WPC) placed portions of Western and Central New York under a Marginal Risk in its Excessive Rainfall Outlook (ERO) due to an moisture-rich air mass interacting with localized convergence boundaries. NWS Buffalo's Area Forecast Discussions highlighted that high precipitable water values, combined with slow-moving convective cells, created an environment capable of producing high rainfall rates over short durations. As afternoon thunderstorms developed along lake breezes and terrain features across the Southern Tier and Finger Lakes, storm motion slowed enough to cause localized rainfall accumulations of 2 to 3+ inches in isolated pockets. Consequently, the primary hydrological impacts observed were localized flash flooding, small-stream rises, and urban drainage ponding in flood-prone, low-lying areas.
episodes.216894: A weak upper trough sat over southwest Louisiana for multiple days. This allowed scattered diurnal storms to develop with a couple storms becoming severe.
episodes.216934: A broad upper trough and weak surface low combined with strong heating to result in scattered thunderstorm development across eastern Virginia.

A couple of the areas most impacted by flash flooding include Dixonville in Indiana county, where 25 homes had basement flooding and in Dawson in Fayette county where the first floor and basements of some homes were flooded and damage occurred to several private bridges.
episodes.217001: Supercells and a QLCS thunderstorm complex developed during the afternoon and evening hours resulting in multiple reports of large hail and widespread damaging winds.
